en: The Śramaṇa Ji composed this treatise.
Thus, the four conditions are established across fifteen locations. The commentary states: Within the response regarding the conditions, there are two parts.
Having already analyzed above the four types of productive conditions for conceptualization, [the author now proceeds] himself...
Below, following the sequential vehicle, the establishment of the ten causes based on the conditions and bases is explained.
This section has three parts;
first, these four conditions are based upon fifteen bases and so forth.
Having explained that the preceding four conditions are taught as ten causes based on fifteen points, the inquiry arises for the following section.
Second is the formal response;
third is the summary. Having concluded this incidental discussion, one should now address the main argument.
This is the first [point].
To clarify the sense that the four conditions encompass all phenomena exhaustively, they are established separately.
In the response below, there are four [sections].
First, it clarifies how the ten causes are established based on fifteen locations.
Second, it distinguishes how the ten causes are subsumed within the two causes.
Third, it clarifies the establishment of the four conditions based on the locations and so forth.
The ten causes and two causes are mutually inclusive.

Fourth, it clarifies that the four conditions, based on their respective bases and so forth, yield various amounts of results. Furthermore, another interpretation states that this current section establishes the thesis:
while the meanings of the four conditions are distinct, they are established as ten causes based upon fifteen bases.
In the following explanation, first,
ten causes are established based on fifteen locations;
next, it is explained upon which locations the four conditions are established, and so forth.
The subsequent discussion on the attainment of the fruit concerns the subsumption of the ten causes and the two causes; however,
these are merely ancillary meanings of the ten causes in the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*).
Therefore, it is not a separate category. The treatise states:
"From the single locus of speech up to the nature of the speech produced."
The commentary states:
This sets forth the essence of the bases (*āśraya*).
Regarding the term "bases":
It is not a separate entity from its cause;
rather, "speech" (*vāc*) is the locus of reliance.
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (locative determinative compound).
The same applies to all subsequent cases.
It is of one essence with its cause;
however, "basis" (āśraya) is used here in a figurative sense.
The seventh case ending (*saptamī-vibhakti*) is established upon the very substance of speech to signify the sense of "reason for designation" (*prajñapti-hetu*) and so forth.

This cause is explained in the *Mahā-śāstra* (Yogācārabhūmi) chapter 5, chapter 38, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* chapter 18, and the *Abhidharma-samuccaya* chapter 4; it is discussed in both the *Madhyānta-vibhāga* and the aforementioned texts.
However, in the *Mahā-śāstra* chapter 38...
There are only three kinds of ten causes,
and the five fruits are subsumed within the category of "without a basis" (anāśrita).
In the Abhidharma, there is only the name "ten causes."
Nor is it exhaustive. In the first part of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, chapter eighteen, there are ten causes;
subsequently, the bases for these causes are analyzed.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle five, in its analysis of the basis of causes (*hetv-adhiṣṭhāna*), does not explain the cause separately.
Furthermore, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
"In accordance with all phenomena, because names come first, there is perception (*saṃjñā*)."
It is taught because perception (*saṃjñā*) precedes it;
that is, perception is the cause for the conventional designation of those various phenomena.
According to the force of that treatise, it appears as if the three factors—perception, conceptualization, and speech—are taken as the essential nature of the cause for designating all phenomena.
However, this present text correctly explains that intention:
it takes only the speech arising from the three factors—phenomena (*dharma*), names (*nāman*), and conceptualizations (*saṃjñā*)—as the essence of this cause. Why is this so?
Since this cause is established based on the locus of speech and words,
its intrinsic nature is exclusively speech.
Otherwise, it would have to be said that this cause is established based on the loci of names, concepts, and discourse.
In this context, all phenomena themselves constitute the fruit;
name, concept, and discourse serve as the supporting causes.
Discourse is precisely the cause for the expression of all phenomena.
"Speech" refers to the nature of speech;
"the nature of speech" is a general term that encompasses all three natures, having vocal action as its essence.
Only the Buddha is virtuous;
all others are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Nevertheless, because there is representation (*vijñapti*), speech can be said to be either virtuous or non-virtuous.
However, in reality, there are two natures;
although "name" and "word" are merely distinctions in terminology,
because they lack denotation, they do not correspond to their respective designations.
Speech is of the nature of karma;
with the exception of the Buddha, all names are indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Alternatively, it may be held that in the Mahāyāna, there is no substance apart from sound.
Therefore, the name itself applies to all three natures.
However, because the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and their acquisition (*prāpti*) are cited as examples to show they share the same substratum (*āśraya*),
one cannot claim that the characteristic is a common cause (*sādhāraṇa-hetu*) in the same way as the name.
Because the meaning of the common cause (sādhāraṇa-hetu) is universally applicable throughout the Mahāyāna,
the treatise establishes the cause of conventional designation (anuvāda-hetu) based on this very point.
The commentary states:
This explains that the reason (hetu) is established based upon words and based upon conventional designations;
it is not a separate entity.
This establishes the meaning based upon the substance.
The treatise states: "It means that by relying on these words, one explains various meanings."
The commentary states:

This explanation establishes the meaning of the "reason for teaching" (*deśanā-hetu*) based on linguistic expression; that is to say, it refers to that which designates all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*).
Names are derived from their characteristics;
only then do verbal expressions arise.
It is based on these words that one subsequently engages in seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing.
Alternatively, because various meanings are explained in accordance with what is seen by others and so forth,
the reason is established based on the words.
[Treatise]
"This is precisely that which can speak [the cause] for what is spoken.
The commentary states: "This explains the meaning of 'cause' (hetu)."
What serves as the cause?
It is this very speech that is capable of expression,
which serves as the cause for all phenomena that are expressed.
The ancient masters said that it is not the case that all dharmas spoken of constitute the substance of this cause.
If that were so, then speech itself would be the result;
thus, seeing, hearing, and so forth [would also be results].
As stated in the *Nin-jū-san* (The Ninety-three), the first chapter of the *Abhidharma*, and the *Shu-yō* (Essential Points) and other commentaries:
the term "following" (*anuvartate*) carries the meaning of "pursuing" or "conforming."
One immediately gives rise to speech and makes utterances in accordance with what has been seen, heard, and so forth.

The *Mahā-śāstra* and other texts are all consistent with this passage. However, this refers to the "cause of conventional expression" (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*) that is both impure (*sāsrava*) and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The fruit (phala) encompasses all conditioned and unconditioned, as well as contaminated and uncontaminated, phenomena;
this is in the sense of a descriptive compound (karmadhāraya), because the indeterminate itself is the cause.
Since the indeterminate is taken as the fruit,
the discourse that characterizes it as indeterminate is said to have the indeterminate as its cause.
This is according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) interpretation.
If the former explanation holds that the cause consists only of the tainted (*sāsrava*) and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
the latter explanation extends to being subsumed under all three natures, both tainted and untainted (*anāsrava*).
The causes for defilement and purification can be understood by analogy with this.
The treatise states: "Some treatises explain that these [factors] persist until they arise accordingly."
The commentary states:

This [position] contradicts the assembly [of scriptures]. As for those who hold the view that it is "conceptualization" (*saṃjñā*), the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* explains that it is "like names and so forth."
This is the commentary on that [verse].
This cause has the three factors of name (*nāman*), conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), and view (*dṛṣṭi*) as its intrinsic nature.
That is to say, the two factors of conceptualization and view apprehend the characteristics of objects in the manner of expressive names.
And there arises attachment.
Attachment to the grasping of signs occurs through views;
for once one has given rise to the grasping of signs according to names, one subsequently gives rise to verbal expression.
That which is spoken as being produced with those three factors as its causes is its fruit.
Treatise:
If one relies on that explanation, it extends to this locus of speech.
The commentary states:
According to that text,
the nature consists of these three dharmas.
The three factors together with speech as their basis are called the "basis of speech" (*vāg-āśraya*).
This term "basis of speech" is also explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.
If one follows this interpretation,
it reveals that this [designation] is the cause of name, conception,
and view, and is the basis for speech.
Because the three dharmas constitute the causal substance. Question: For what reason do these two treatises contradict one another? Answer: The intent of the two treatises differs.
Although there is no explicit reconciliation between the treatises, I shall now explain the meaning according to my own interpretation.
In works such as the *Mahā-śāstra*,
all phenomena (*dharma*) are treated as effects and explained as causes;
in terms of that which is expressed (*vācya*), it is the effect of that which expresses (*vācaka*).
Thus, the two— subject and object— are explained as cause and effect.
In the Abhidharma, Asaṅga takes "arising" (utpāda) as cause and effect,
because verbal expression arises based on name (nāman), concept (saṃjñā), and view (dṛṣṭi).
Nor are they contradictory, as each is based on a single specific meaning.
Thus, the Abhidharma states: "The efficient cause is explained according to [its specific] function."
"Following what is said" refers to speech.
The "capacities for following what is said" are name, concept, and view.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Da lun) explains [the nature of] causes by means of penetrating all phenomena and characterizing objects;
the *Abhidharma* (Dui fa), however, explains results solely based on the arising of defiled factors.
Thus, there is no contradiction between them.
Treatise:
From the "basis for experience" up to "the nature of that which is experienced and that which experiences.
Commentary states:
"Contemplation" (guan) refers to facing [the object];
"waiting" (dai) refers to relying upon it.
This means that this cause pervades both the subject and the object.
However, it is the sensations of subject and object that are metaphorically relied upon which constitute the "remainder," and not others.
Yet, some say that only the three sensations constitute its essence;
this is not so, for [the act of] seeking to eat and so forth also depends upon food and other such factors.
That which is awaited as food is the cause of desire;
if one seeks food and drink only after waiting for sensual desire,
then feeling (*vedanā*) is the cause of food.
However, the locus of reception encompasses both the agent and the object;
it cannot be called "desire," because desire is not all-pervasive.
Because it is not of the nature of feeling,
one contemplates this very [consciousness] as the capacity that experiences and the object experienced,
which receives the fruit of that which is capable of being experienced.
Alternatively, it may be that "arising," "abiding," "accomplishing," and "attaining" are the causes for that which depends upon them, such as the arising and so forth.
However, the Mahā-śāstras and other texts all state that one seeks or grasps by depending on this.
That which is depended upon and received serves as the cause for seeking and so forth.
As the *Triṃśikā-bhāṣya* (and other texts) state:
"Because one depends on feet, and because feet are the cause, there is the activity of coming and going."
It is not necessarily caused by sensation (*vedanā*),
because that which it depends upon is not sensation.
Furthermore, this treatise states that it pervades both what is experienced and what is not.
However, that which is depended upon here— whether it be the agent of grasping or the object grasped— is all subsumed under this cause.
There are cases where the agent of grasping is taken as the cause,
and the agent of grasping is taken as the result.
Just as suffering is regarded as pleasure [in comparison],
there are cases where that which is capable of being felt is the cause and that which is felt is the result.
There are cases where that which is experienced is the cause and that which is experienced is the result;
there are cases where that which is experienced is the cause.
That which is capable of receiving [an object] constitutes the fruit;
this is distinguished by four propositions.
This is because the dharmas that are received are also termed "reception."
Now, regarding that which is capable of experiencing, we take only the category of feeling (vedanā).
First, it is constant and pervasive throughout all states of mind;
second, it is distinguished by its five functional modes.
Mental factors such as those with specific objects do not constantly and universally accompany all states of mind;
this is because the four factors beginning with attention lack five distinct stages. Although contact (sparśa) is likewise [not constant], [it is nevertheless universal].
However, regarding what is received, it does not belong to oneself;

it is not grasped in the same manner as the act of receiving itself. Within that which is received, all dharmas are included, with the exception of the dharmas that serve as the causal conditions for seeds.
This cause is remote;
only that which is remotely related through mutual dependence constitutes this cause,
as in the case of a seed with respect to a sprout.
Internal seeds, when compared to manifest phenomena, are in all cases not the causes thereof;
otherwise, it would follow that they should be said to obtain results of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), yet they do not so obtain.
Only those that are distantly related obtain [the name "condition"];

that is, those which are closely related are all subsumed under "inducing" (*āvāhaka*), "attracting" (*ākṣepaka*), and so forth. Question: For what reason is it said that the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is subsumed under "attracting" and "arising"?
It is also subsumed under "distinct determination" (*pratiniyama*) and so forth.
The statement that the "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*) is "contingency" (*apekṣā*) is further subsumed under "projecting" (*ākṣepa*) and so forth.
What fault is there in this? The answer is: it is not so.
Because the name [of the object] is remote.
That which is called "contingent upon" (apekṣā) must necessarily be something that is not proximate.

Because the names of causes such as "distinct determination" (pratiniyama) apply to their characteristics in common; furthermore, another interpretation holds that even those which are directly dependent [upon one another] are also this cause, because in the following discussion of these effects, the author refers only to those that are remote and does not mention those that are direct.
It does not state that it obtains a fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) and so forth;
this interpretation is superior. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that "regarding" (*apekṣā*) means "observing";
that is, the object must depend upon the mental faculty.
Sentience (*cetanā*) is that which, in dependence upon an object, constitutes the nature of the agent and the recipient;

since a seed in relation to a sprout is not a case of sentience observing in dependence [upon an object], it is not this cause. Question: If that is so, why is it said that because they serve as causes, there are karmas of coming and going? Answer: These too are internal phenomena (*adhyātma-dharma*) insofar as they are depended upon by sentience.
Phenomena such as sprouts arising from causes and conditions do not depend upon sentient beings;
for the time at which they depend upon sentient beings is not a cause or condition.
This is the correct meaning explained previously.
Since that which is received takes that which is awaited as its cause,
the sprout’s awaiting of the seed may likewise be considered this cause;
furthermore, it is a neutral (avyākṛta) cause.
If that which is indeterminate (avyākṛta) is a cause, it is exclusively with outflows (sāsrava).
However, an indeterminate fruit may be either with or without outflows (anāsrava), and may consist of dharmas of any of the three natures (trividha-svabhāva).
If the fruit is indeterminate...
It takes the indeterminate as its cause; that is,
while its causes may pertain to all three natures— defiled, undefiled, or indeterminate—
its fruit is exclusively indeterminate.
The remaining defiled factors and so forth should all be understood according to this principle.
In this very context, the treatise establishes the dependence-condition (*apekṣā-hetu*).
The commentary states:
This explains the establishment of the cause based upon the locus.
Treatise:
This refers to the "condition as dependence" (*apekṣā-hetu*), which means that depending on this, one reaches that.
The commentary states:
The meaning of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and other treatises is the same as this.
This demonstrates that the observation of dependence regarding cause and effect operates in four instances,
excluding only the immediate causal condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). Treatise:
"Because the three types of habitual tendencies (vāsanā) persist until they reach their own distant results.
The commentary states:
This refers to the stage when internal and external seeds have not yet reached maturation.
This refers to all seeds— whether contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), internal or external—
that have not yet been moistened by the power of spiritual friends and the like,
but are instead moistened by craving and so forth.
That which is moistened by water, earth,
and so forth is all termed the basis of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*),
because [it was] not yet moistened at the time [prior to being moistened].
However, because it can project its own distant fruit,
regardless of whether its nature is identical or different, that which corresponds to it is called "its own fruit" (*svaphala*). For instance,
within the category of pure causes (*śuddha-hetu*):
It serves as a remote cause for the pure dharmas that can realize nirvāṇa;
do not see the statements in the *Mahāśāstra* and other texts as implying that this cause is a direct cause for the realization of nirvāṇa as purity.
He then says that this fruit is an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma,
because the unconditioned is remote and not produced by causes,
and because the treatise does not state that there is a fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*).
Now, this cause is proximate;
the causes and effects of these three natures follow the nature of their respective causes,
because they are produced directly by causal conditions and produced through predominant influence.
Because it can induce results of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) and dominant results (*adhipati-phala*).
Alternatively, even among the causes of defilement, there is a difference in the nature of the result,
namely, the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
The fruit is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta),
while the cause may be either wholesome (kuśala) or unwholesome (akuśala).
If it is indeterminate, it is then the cause.
The fruit is exclusively indeterminate.
If it is untainted, then the cause and fruit are both exclusively untainted.
Wholesome and unwholesome [dharmas] are the causes;
their fruits encompass all three natures. As for neutral causes:
The cause permeates all three natures,
while the fruit is exclusively indeterminate;
this should be reflected upon according to reason.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other treatises state:
"The fourth is the basis for seeds that possess moisture, because it is proximate to its own fruit."
The commentary states:
That aforementioned seed, once moistened by the power of virtuous friends and other factors, is termed "having moisture as its basis," because it is capable of producing proximate fruits.
It is that which, as a pure cause, serves as the causal condition for being near to enlightenment.
In this context, it differs only from what was previously moistened or not yet moistened;
it has no separate essence.
The nature of the fruit and so forth are all the same as before;
the *Mahāśāstra* and other texts are likewise. Treatise:
"The five [factors] that have ceased immediately prior serve as the basis for the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Commentary:
This refers specifically to the equal-and-immediate condition of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
It takes mind and mental factors as its fruit.
This condition has been explained previously.
Regarding the nature [of the cause], whichever nature it may follow, the fruit is common to all three natures; however, each is exclusively its own consciousness.
Because it has only mind and mental factors as its essence.
Treatise:
From the six objective spheres and bases up to the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The commentary states:
Its essence pervades all phenomena;
its fruit consists solely of mind and mental factors.
The contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) [dharmas] and so forth all pertain to both cause and effect.
If the future is taken as the cause, [it is as follows].
If the fruit were not present,
it would not be the case that the cause precedes and the fruit follows;
this is likewise not so now.
The objective aspect (nimittabhāga) manifests as future objects while being present;
since there is no real future, the object-condition (ālambanapratyaya) never exists without its fruit.
These thirty-eight [factors] are explained as the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya).
And as for the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya),
it applies only with respect to all minds and mental factors (citta-caitta). Thus says the treatise.
"The locus of the seven faculties extends to the six faculties that serve as their bases.
The commentary states:
"Their substance consists of the six faculties."
This refers to all eight consciousnesses;
its substance consists of the five sense organs.
Its fruit is exclusively mind and mental factors.
The nature of the fruition of the first three fruits is identical;
their causes may be inferred accordingly. However, regarding the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*):
This means that it serves as a condition at the present time, not in the past;
for the past no longer exists.
Thus, it is the present that possesses causal efficacy.
Because it can guide and lead the Dharma so that it arises in the future,
its function is only manifested when entering the past,
for at that time the fruit becomes manifest.
Because the locus is empty. The treatise states:
from the eight bases of functional activity up to the other auxiliary manifest conditions.
The commentary states:
This refers to the activity of the instrument with respect to the action to be performed,
such as the function of cutting or felling possessed by tools like adzes and axes.
Regarding "excluding the seeds, the remaining auxiliary manifest conditions":
this refers to excluding the production of manifest phenomena from internal and external seeds, as well as the production of seeds from seeds.
The seeds manifesting in the present life and the immediate auxiliary conditions are [the direct causes],
while all other dharmas are the remote auxiliary conditions.
Treatise:
From the nine bases of human effort (*puruṣakāra-adhiṣṭhāna*) up to their acting as present conditions for others.
Commentary states:
This refers to the activity of the agent with respect to the action being performed; specifically,
it refers to the primary auxiliary condition that directly assists the principal agent who is currently performing the action, as distinguished from those previously excluded.
The breadth and narrowness of its fruit are the same as those previously described.
This is because the activity (*kāritra*) and the *puruṣakāra-phala* must necessarily be identical to that which is produced;
therefore, the direct [cause] is not taken [as the basis].
It is not because of [specific] causes and conditions.
These two fruits encompass both the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), as well as the three natures; their causes are likewise so.
However, these two and the previous five indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) states are themselves the causes.
Excluding the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the sense-faculties as bases (*indriya-āśraya*),
the remaining bases and their fruits are both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Those two fruits are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).
Since their two causes are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
they do not give rise to the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
This is formulated based on the six consciousnesses.
If the seventh or eighth consciousnesses serve as the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
then the indeterminate [state] is the cause.
The fruits include both the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the seven tainted (*sāsrava*) faculties,
because six are untainted.
It acts as the cause for the indeterminate,
excluding the immediate condition and the faculties.
Other causes are common to both the out-flowing (sāsrava) and the non-out-flowing (anāsrava), as well as all three natures (tridhātu).
This discussion is based on the six consciousnesses;
however, if one relies on the seventh consciousness, the out-flowing can arise immediately after the non-out-flowing.
The cause of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)—
its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) as a cause— is also common to the untainted (*anāsrava*);
this should be distinguished among the faculties (*indriya*).
Because the physical faculties and the mental faculty each have their own distinct natures,
the term "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*) used herein refers exclusively to the activity of sentient beings as persons.
Therefore, the passage below states only that it obtains the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), and does not state that it obtains fruits such as disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*).
Here, too, the term "beings" includes both internal and external entities, not merely internal sentient beings.
However, both *kāritra* (activity) and *puruṣakāra* (human effort) are expressed in the third case;
in Sanskrit, this is called *karaṇa*,
which signifies the instrument of action.
The kalala is the activity of the person;
therefore, the two are distinct.
However, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 38:
It is said that all conditions other than the seed are termed "appropriation" (parigraha);
since this [condition] merely assists in the accomplishment of appropriation,
the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) is excluded.
Just as when visual consciousness arises,
it takes the eye faculty and its seeds as its efficient cause (puruṣakāra-āśraya).
The equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), and so forth serve as the basis for its activity,
because the faculties are slightly more proximate.
This is explained in terms of the "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*) of dharmas.
If a person is designated as a "functioning agent" (puruṣakāra) with respect to a thing and not with respect to a dharma,
one should understand this by analogy with the case of a person in relation to grain or a sprout.
Human effort constitutes the primary cause,
while earth, water, and so forth constitute the contributory conditions;
for these latter are more remote than human exertion.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, among the thirty-eight types of indeterminate causes (*avyākṛta-hetu*), all possess human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
In these cases, earth, water, and so forth constitute the human effort,
while the sun and the act of tilling constitute the functional activity (*kāritra*).
Treatise:
From the "Ten Bases for the Vision of Reality" up to the "Aids for Adducing Proof.
Commentary states:
This refers to all untainted views (*anāsrava-dṛṣṭi*).

With the exception of the seeds produced by the self-perfuming of the causes and effects of those views themselves, they serve as causes for all unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena; in relation to all others, they are entirely such causes.
That which induces by means of causes and conditions is subsumed under the inducing cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*);
it assists the co-arising dharmas that are untainted and conditioned,
enabling them to perform their functions in concert.
Or, because it causes [the wholesome roots] to increase,
it is capable of inducing uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) existence in the future;
this refers to the principle that a preceding factor induces a subsequent one.
That which is capable of realization serves as the cause for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This reveals the supreme fruit.
[End of] Treatise.
This is because, based on these six in total, one proceeds to the analysis of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The commentary states:
"The preceding six bases are the essence of the causes for appropriation."
Because the first five are comprised within the remote object of appropriation (*parigraha*),
they bring about the accomplishment of all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena of the three realms;
if the sixth is also comprised within the remote object of appropriation, it brings about the accomplishment of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena.
This refers to the sixth basis, which does not pertain to the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*).
It is called "appropriation" (*parigraha*) because it assists as a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Therefore, it excludes those causal conditions that are directly capable of producing phenomena.
Therefore, the Abhidharma says:
it is like the field, water, fertilizer, and so forth,

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there would otherwise be no objects for the five kinds of mental factors;
since they do possess objects,

The same principle applies to all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). However, according to the intention of the former masters, each [factor] takes as its object the seeds transformed by itself;
yet, it is only the seeds transformed by the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) that can produce actual manifestations (*pravṛtti*).
It is not that which is transformed by the five [sense organs],
just as the eye-faculty and so forth lack the function of producing consciousness.
This master objects, saying:
Why is it that a single object of cognition is divided into two meanings?
The eighth [consciousness] and the five [sensory consciousnesses] lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The former master explains as follows:
If there must necessarily be a substantial basis (ālambana-pratyaya),
then when the sixth consciousness takes empty space as its object, what serves as that basis? Furthermore,
the eighth mind-king does not arise by depending on the objects of the five [sensory] categories.
How can they share the same objective basis (*ālambana-vastu*)?
Some say that all consciousnesses must rely upon an objective basis to arise;
for example, when taking space as its object, it relies upon the name "space" as its objective basis.
The eighth mind-king arises with the fivefold transformed appearances as its substantial basis by virtue of their provisional power;
thus, it is said that the name and the object of cognition are identical. Treatise.
If it is granted that the color changes until it becomes a different substance,

Regarding the five objects:
the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) also necessarily takes seeds as its object;

Therefore, the former master’s position is truly worthy of appreciation. Thus says the treatise.

Since the first section above has already been explained,

Furthermore, there are those who interpret it as follows:
because it was stated in the preceding text that one must not see the objective spheres of the [subjective] divisions as being of different substance,

The self-cognizing aspect (svasaṃvitti) takes only internal conditions as its object and does not transform further into something else;

However, these are both subsumed within the image aspect (nimittabhāga).
Because associated mental factors (saṃprayuktadharma) are likewise external objects of apprehension,
and since these associated factors do not externally apprehend a distinct objective aspect (nimittabhāga) when taking consciousness as their object,
it follows by analogy that the same must hold true for the subjective aspect (darśanabhāga) of consciousness.
Furthermore, this does not contradict the aforementioned point that the objects of the seeing-part (darśanabhāga) are identical.
Although this interpretation is superior, it is somewhat difficult to understand.

acting as an image-condition (*pratibimba-pratyaya*), it remains nonetheless a representational division (*nimitta-bhāga*).
If it were not so, it would be no different from the self-cognizing consciousness (*svasaṃvedana*);
why, then, would four divisions be necessary?
Therefore, every state of mind possesses all four divisions.
Now, the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) of the associated dharma takes the self-witnessing-part (svasaṃvedana-bhāga) as its object,
and it is also able to take the part that witnesses the self-witnessing-part (svasaṃvittisākṣātkāra-bhāga) as its object.
As for the self-witnessing division (svasaṃvittibhāga) being able to take the seeing division (darśanabhāga) and the image division (nimittabhāga) as its objects:
this occurs only at the stage of Buddhahood; others cannot do so.
In this context, it is merely intended to exclude the possibility that the seeing division is not an object of the image division.
The meaning excludes the third [alternative]. The four parts (*catur-bhāga*) are also not objects of perception by way of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
This indicates that the remaining three parts mutually take all phenomena as their objects;
thus, they are called "universal objects" (*sarvālambana*).
Even if one makes this interpretation, how are the three parts distinguished?
Since each is similar [to the others],

thus, a distinction is established. Furthermore, it is interpreted that here we merely negate that the *nimitta-bhāga* (the image-part) can serve as the objective condition (*ālambana*), and negate that the *darśana-bhāga* (the seeing-part) takes the self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) as its object.

This is because these two conditions occupy a middle position among the four conditions;
that is, they can only produce their effects—namely, mind and mental factors—by depending upon them.

Because it is not a perfuming agent;
because its essence cannot be distinguished from that which is not its own direct seed; and because, apart from its own seed, [it lacks such a relationship].

Merit is the ultimate reality,
because both its intrinsic nature and its fruit possess the excellence of being desirable.

because their characteristics are base and inferior.
"Immovable" (āniñjya) means that it cannot be altered or transformed.
Because its karma remains fixed upon a single object without wavering;
furthermore, even when shifting between objects— as occurs with innate or acquired mundane virtues—

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that wholesome karma bound to the desire realm is called "merit" (*puṇya*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says:
That which brings about maturation in the happy realms,
as well as wholesome karma conducive to experience within the five destinies, is called merit (*puṇya*).
The former refers to the general karma for humans and devas.
The latter refers to the distinct karma of the five destinies (*pañcagati*).
However, it is taught that even in the hells there is distinct wholesome karma that results in an outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*),

Karma that is distinct from and similar [to its result] is called wholesome (*kuśala*).
Furthermore, karma that causes the various sufferings of hell to become slight is called wholesome karma,
such as not severing the roots of goodness (*akuśalamūla*) and so forth.
Furthermore, if discussed in terms of the six destinies,
excluding the hells and the asuras,
the five destinies possess the fruits of wholesome karma. As for non-meritorious karma:
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "That is to say,
it refers to that which brings about the maturation of the miserable realms (*apāya*),
as well as that which is conducive to the maturation of the five destinies (*gati*)."
The former refers to the general karma for the three evil destinies;

the latter refers to the specific karma for the five destinies. "Imperturbable" (*āniñjya*) refers to karma that brings about maturation in the form and formless realms, as well as karma conducive to feeling in the form and formless realms; the former is general karma.
The latter refers to distinct karma.
The Abhidharma-śāstra asks:
For what reason are the karmas of the form and formless realms called "immovable"?
Answer: Just as karma from other destinies in the desire realm may,
upon encountering conditions, be transformed to be experienced in another destiny or location,
that [specific] karma is not like that.
Because it is experienced within its own sphere.
Question: Why is this so? Answer: Because it is comprised within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This is not the same as scattered karma.
If that were so, how could karma perfumed by dhyāna—which is inferior—give rise to birth in the five Pure Abodes?
Therefore, this explanation is incorrect. Furthermore, that which is comprised within the stage of meditative concentration (samāhitabhūmi) is called "immovable" (āniñjya).
Because concentration (*samādhi*) is able to abide upon a single object,
the designation "merit" (*puṇya*) should apply generally to the completing karma (*pūrṇakarma*) of all three realms. Furthermore,
superior wholesome karma that possesses a distinct and preeminent capacity is specifically termed "unshakable" (*āneñjya*).
This is the general name obtained for the various types of wholesome karma in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
However, regarding the specific karma conducive to experience within the "unshakable" (*āniñjya*) states, there is a slight difference in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*,
as explained in its commentaries.
However, these three types of karma pertain to body, speech, and mind.
Mental karma pervades all three realms;
bodily and vocal karma exist only in two stages.
Because it is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra,
its essential nature consists of the two types of volition— wholesome and unwholesome— that are associated with outflows; these constitute the substance of this karma.
Because they involve the movement of the body and the movement of speech, they are called "karma.
Body and speech themselves are exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*),
as they do not possess the nature of being wholesome or unwholesome.
It has volition alone as its essence.
In this context, does it have volition alone as its activity,
or is there something else?

Treatise:
"The perfuming of the fundamental consciousness is termed 'habitual energy' (*vāsanā*).
Commentary: [As follows].
When an active karma is being performed,
it perfumes the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), giving rise to a functional capacity for that specific karma.
This functional capacity is precisely what is referred to in the verse as "habitual tendencies" (vāsanā).
Why is it called "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*)?
The treatise states:
It is so named because it is a portion of the momentum of karma that reaches [its fruition].
The commentary states:
This is a portion of the energy of karma;
it is explained as the energy of liberation, which is formed through present perfuming.

Regarding the analysis of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*): these karmas are perfumed differently; those who lack a sense of shame (*ahrikya*) reckon that all karma is produced by past actions, asserting that everything is merely what has previously existed.
The Mahīśāsaka school and others maintain that karma enters the past while still possessing substantial reality (*dravya*) in the present.
Furthermore, this "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*) distinguishes itself from the Sarvāstivādins' view that past karma possesses a real substance;
it also distinguishes itself from the Lokāyata materialists' claim that all results are obtained solely through present karma and are experienced at the very moment they are performed.
Now, this principle regarding habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) is not so.
Because the manifest activity (*samudācāra*) of the immediately preceding past moment perfumes [the consciousness],
the seeds perish in each preceding moment and arise in each succeeding moment, thus existing constantly in the present.
Therefore, setting aside those [karmas] that were functional in previous lives— which possess a present substantial entity as their karma—
this very seed does not receive its fruit at the time it is produced;
rather, it receives its fruit only later, whether after one lifetime, many years, or even many lifetimes.
Therefore, when the present action is performed, its fruit is received immediately.
